questions.q: What does a tokenizer hand to an LLM as its actual input?
options: A fixed-length sentence embedding vector
A one-hot matrix over the alphabet
A sequence of integer token IDs
A list of lemmatized words
questions.why: The tokenizer splits text into vocabulary units and maps each to an integer ID; the model's embedding layer then turns those IDs into vectors. A sentence embedding is something a model produces, not what a tokenizer feeds it.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of subword tokenization over word-level tokenization?
options: Rare or unseen words can be built from known pieces with a manageable vocabulary
It always produces fewer tokens than word-level tokenization
It removes the need for special tokens
It makes tokenization language-specific and therefore more accurate
questions.why: Subword schemes keep frequent words whole and split rare words into frequent fragments, which nearly eliminates out-of-vocabulary problems without a huge vocabulary. They usually produce slightly *more* tokens than word-level splitting, not fewer.

questions.q: A developer considers character-level tokenization to avoid any unknown tokens. What is the main drawback?
options: It cannot represent punctuation
It requires a vocabulary of millions of entries
It cannot be decoded back to text
Sequences become much longer, increasing compute and consuming the context window
questions.why: Character vocabularies are tiny, but every word becomes many tokens, so the same text uses several times more positions and attention compute. The vocabulary is small, not huge, which is the opposite of option B.

questions.q: How does Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary during training?
options: It starts with whole words and splits the least frequent ones
It starts with characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair
It clusters word embeddings and assigns one token per cluster
It keeps the subwords that maximize a unigram language-model likelihood
questions.why: BPE is a bottom-up merge algorithm: each learned merge becomes a new vocabulary entry until the target vocabulary size is reached. Option D describes the Unigram algorithm, which works top-down by pruning.

questions.q: A BERT tokenizer splits "playing" into `play` and `##ing`. What does the `##` indicate?
options: The token is a padding marker
The token is a special control token
The token continues the previous token rather than starting a new word
The token was unknown and replaced
questions.why: WordPiece marks word-internal pieces with `##` so the original word boundaries can be reconstructed on decoding. Unknown words become `[UNK]`, not `##` pieces.

questions.q: What distinguishes SentencePiece from tokenizers that require pre-tokenization on whitespace?
options: It treats input as a raw character stream and encodes spaces as a symbol (▁), making it language-independent
It only works for English text
It splits text strictly on punctuation
It uses a fixed vocabulary of 256 bytes with no merges
questions.why: Because SentencePiece does not assume words are separated by spaces, it works for languages like Japanese and Chinese and makes detokenization lossless. It is a framework that can run BPE or Unigram; it is not restricted to raw bytes.

questions.q: How does the Unigram tokenization algorithm arrive at its final vocabulary?
options: By merging the most frequent character pairs
By greedily matching the longest prefix in a dictionary
By assigning one token per Unicode code point
By starting from a large candidate vocabulary and pruning tokens whose removal least hurts corpus likelihood
questions.why: Unigram is top-down: it scores segmentations with a unigram language model and iteratively removes low-value tokens. Merging frequent pairs is BPE's bottom-up approach.

questions.q: Why does byte-level BPE (as in GPT-2) never need an `<unk>` token?
options: It lowercases all text before encoding
Its base vocabulary contains all 256 byte values, so any string can be encoded
It drops characters it does not recognize
It has a vocabulary of every Unicode character
questions.why: Every UTF-8 string is a sequence of bytes, so in the worst case text falls back to individual byte tokens. Including every Unicode character would need a vocabulary of well over 100,000 base symbols, which is exactly what byte-level BPE avoids.

questions.q: A legacy word-level tokenizer encounters a word not in its vocabulary. What typically happens?
options: The word is mapped to a single unknown token, losing its content
The word is split into characters automatically
The tokenizer raises an exception and stops
The word is added to the vocabulary on the fly
questions.why: Word-level vocabularies are fixed after training, so any unseen word collapses to `<unk>` and the model cannot tell different unknown words apart. Falling back to smaller pieces is precisely what subword tokenizers add.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off when increasing a tokenizer's vocabulary size?
options: More unknown tokens but faster training
Longer sequences but a smaller model
Shorter sequences but larger embedding and output layers
Better multilingual support but no effect on model size
questions.why: A bigger vocabulary packs more text into each token, saving context and compute per character, but the embedding matrix and output projection grow with vocabulary size. Rare tokens in a huge vocabulary may also be under-trained.

questions.q: Using the common rule of thumb for English text with GPT-style tokenizers, roughly how many tokens is a 750-word document?
options: About 190 tokens
About 750 tokens
About 3,000 tokens
About 1,000 tokens
questions.why: A common heuristic is that one token is about four characters, or about 0.75 English words, so 750 words is roughly 1,000 tokens. 3,000 would correspond to counting characters/4 incorrectly or using character-level tokenization; the exact number should always be checked with the model's tokenizer.

questions.q: What role does the end-of-sequence (EOS) token play during generation?
options: It separates the system prompt from the user prompt
It signals that the model has finished, so the generation loop stops
It marks padding positions
It indicates an unknown character
questions.why: When the model samples the EOS token, the decoder treats the sequence as complete. Padding uses a separate pad token (sometimes set equal to EOS for convenience, but with a different purpose).

questions.q: In a padded batch, what does a value of 0 in the `attention_mask` tell the model?
options: This position is padding and should be ignored
This position is the first token of the sequence
This token should be masked for the MLM objective
This token has zero probability of being generated
questions.why: The attention mask has 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding so pad positions do not influence attention. It is unrelated to BERT-style masked-language-model masking, which replaces tokens with `[MASK]`.

questions.q: A team notices that the same paragraph costs three times more tokens in Thai than in English with their LLM. What is the most likely reason?
options: The model uses a larger context window for Thai
Thai text is automatically translated before tokenization
The tokenizer was trained mostly on English, so Thai splits into many short pieces
Thai requires additional special tokens per sentence
questions.why: Tokenizer merges reflect the training corpus; under-represented languages get few merges and fall back to characters or bytes. This inflates cost, latency and context usage for those languages.

questions.q: What are the logits produced by an LLM at each generation step?
options: The probabilities of each token, summing to 1
The embedding vector of the next token
The attention weights of the last layer
Unnormalized scores for every token in the vocabulary
questions.why: The final linear layer outputs one raw score per vocabulary entry. They become probabilities only after softmax, so option A describes the post-softmax distribution, not logits.

questions.q: What does the softmax function do in the decoding pipeline?
options: Selects the single best token
Converts logits into a probability distribution over the vocabulary
Removes low-probability tokens
Normalizes the input text before tokenization
questions.why: Softmax exponentiates and normalizes logits so they are positive and sum to 1. Choosing a token (argmax or sampling) and filtering tokens (top-k/top-p) are separate steps applied afterward.

questions.q: What does greedy decoding do at each step?
options: Selects the highest-probability token
Samples a token in proportion to its probability
Keeps several candidate sequences
Picks randomly among the top 50 tokens
questions.why: Greedy decoding takes the argmax every step, which is deterministic and fast but can miss sequences that are better overall. Keeping several candidates is beam search.

questions.q: How does beam search differ from greedy decoding?
options: It samples randomly from the full distribution
It uses a draft model to propose tokens
It tracks the top-N partial sequences by cumulative log-probability at each step
It generates all tokens in parallel in one step
questions.why: Beam search keeps N "beams" and expands each, retaining the best N overall, so it can find higher-likelihood sequences than greedy. It is still deterministic; a draft model is speculative decoding.

questions.q: A developer lowers the sampling temperature from 1.0 to 0.2. What is the expected effect?
options: More creative and diverse outputs
Longer responses
Higher chance of rare tokens
More focused, near-deterministic outputs
questions.why: Low temperature sharpens the distribution so the most likely tokens dominate. Temperature does not directly control length; higher temperature is what boosts rare tokens.

questions.q: At which point in decoding is temperature applied?
options: To the token IDs before embedding
Logits are divided by the temperature before softmax
To the attention scores in every layer
To the probabilities after sampling
questions.why: Scaling logits by 1/T before softmax makes the distribution sharper (T<1) or flatter (T>1). It does not change the attention computation inside the model.

questions.q: What does top-k sampling with k = 40 do?
options: Samples only from the 40 most probable tokens after renormalizing
Generates 40 candidate responses
Limits output to 40 tokens
Keeps tokens whose cumulative probability reaches 40%
questions.why: Top-k truncates the distribution to a fixed number of candidates, removing the long tail of unlikely tokens. A cumulative-probability cutoff is top-p (nucleus) sampling.

questions.q: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling with p = 0.9 do?
options: Keeps the 90 most likely tokens
Removes 10% of the vocabulary at random
Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least 0.9
Sets the temperature to 0.9
questions.why: The nucleus size changes per step: few tokens when the model is confident, many when it is uncertain. A fixed count of tokens is top-k.

questions.q: Users report that answers stop mid-sentence, and the API returns a finish reason of "length". What is the most likely cause?
options: Temperature is too low
A stop sequence matched early
The tokenizer is mismatched
The max_new_tokens (max output tokens) limit is too small
questions.why: A "length" finish reason means generation hit the output-token cap rather than emitting EOS. A stop-sequence match would report a "stop" reason and typically end at a clean boundary.

questions.q: What is a stop sequence in LLM generation?
options: A token that is removed from the vocabulary
A string that, when generated, causes generation to halt
A penalty applied to repeated phrases
The maximum number of tokens allowed
questions.why: Stop sequences let applications end output at a known delimiter (for example "\nUser:"), and the matched text is usually excluded from the response. Output length limits are set separately.

questions.q: What does a model's context window limit?
options: The total number of tokens (input plus generated) the model can attend to at once
Only the number of tokens in the user's prompt
The number of requests a server can handle concurrently
The number of vocabulary entries
questions.why: Prompt tokens and generated tokens share the same window, so a long prompt leaves less room for output. Concurrency is a serving limit, not a model property.

questions.q: Which statement best describes autoregressive generation in a decoder-only LLM?
options: All output tokens are predicted simultaneously in one forward pass
The model first generates the last token and works backward
Each new token is predicted from all previous tokens, appended, and fed back for the next step
The model rewrites the entire output at every step
questions.why: Generation is a loop: predict next token, append it, repeat until EOS or a limit. Parallel all-at-once prediction describes non-autoregressive models, not standard LLMs.

questions.q: What happens during the prefill phase of LLM inference?
options: The model generates one output token at a time
The tokenizer is loaded into GPU memory
The KV cache is cleared for the next request
All prompt tokens are processed in parallel and their keys/values are cached
questions.why: Prefill runs the whole prompt through the model in one pass, filling the KV cache and producing the first output token's logits. One-token-at-a-time generation is the decode phase.

questions.q: Which phase mostly determines time to first token (TTFT) for a long prompt?
options: The decode phase
The prefill phase
Detokenization
Network streaming of later tokens
questions.why: The first token cannot be emitted until the entire prompt has been processed, so TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus queueing). Decode speed governs the time between subsequent tokens instead.

questions.q: What does time per output token (TPOT), also called inter-token latency, measure?
options: The average time between consecutive generated tokens after the first
The time to load the model weights
The total tokens generated per second across all users
The time spent tokenizing the prompt
questions.why: TPOT reflects decode speed as experienced by one user while streaming. Aggregate tokens per second across all users is system throughput, a different metric.

questions.q: An operator wants to serve as many users as possible on a fixed GPU budget for an offline batch summarization job. Which metric should they optimize?
options: Time to first token
Inter-token latency
Throughput (total tokens per second)
Context window size
questions.why: For offline jobs nobody is waiting on an individual response, so maximizing aggregate tokens per second (often with large batches) minimizes cost. TTFT and inter-token latency matter most for interactive chat.

questions.q: What does the KV cache store during generation?
options: The token IDs of the vocabulary
Previously generated text strings
Gradients for each layer
Key and value tensors of previous tokens for every attention layer
questions.why: Caching keys and values means each decode step only computes projections for the newest token instead of reprocessing the full sequence. Gradients are only needed for training.

questions.q: How does KV cache memory scale during inference?
options: It stays constant regardless of sequence length
It grows linearly with sequence length and with batch size
It grows quadratically with vocabulary size
It shrinks as more tokens are generated
questions.why: Each token in each sequence adds one key and one value vector per layer, so memory grows linearly with tokens and concurrent sequences. Vocabulary size affects the output layer, not the KV cache.

questions.q: What is quantization in the context of LLM inference?
options: Representing weights (and possibly activations) with lower-precision numbers to cut memory and speed up inference
Removing layers from the model
Splitting the model across multiple GPUs
Reducing the vocabulary size
questions.why: Moving from FP16 to INT8 or INT4 halves or quarters weight storage with usually modest accuracy loss. Removing layers is pruning/distillation, and multi-GPU splitting is model parallelism.

questions.q: Approximately how much GPU memory do the weights of a 7-billion-parameter model need in FP16?
options: 7 GB
28 GB
14 GB
3.5 GB
questions.why: FP16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so 7B × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB, before KV cache and runtime overhead. 28 GB would be FP32 (4 bytes), and 7 GB would be INT8.

questions.q: Approximately how much memory do the weights of a 70B-parameter model need when quantized to 4 bits?
options: 70 GB
140 GB
35 GB
questions.why: 4 bits is 0.5 bytes per parameter, so 70B × 0.5 ≈ 35 GB (slightly more with quantization scales). 70 GB corresponds to INT8 and 140 GB to FP16.

questions.q: Why do inference servers batch multiple requests together?
options: To reduce the context window per request
To reuse each weight load across many sequences and raise GPU utilization
To make outputs deterministic
To avoid using a KV cache
questions.why: During decode, reading the weights from memory dominates the cost; batching lets one read serve many sequences, greatly increasing throughput. Batching does not make outputs deterministic or remove the need for a KV cache.

questions.q: What does continuous (in-flight) batching do differently from static batching?
options: Requests join and leave the batch at each decode iteration instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish
It pads all requests to the same length
It processes one request at a time
It only batches requests with identical prompts
questions.why: With iteration-level scheduling, a finished sequence frees its slot immediately and a waiting request takes it, so short requests are not held hostage by long ones. Static batching keeps the batch fixed until the longest sequence completes.

questions.q: What does a repetition penalty do during decoding?
options: Stops generation when a phrase repeats
Increases temperature after each step
Lowers the scores of tokens that have already appeared in the context
Removes duplicate tokens from the prompt
questions.why: Penalizing previously seen tokens discourages loops like "the the the" or repeated sentences. It adjusts scores; it does not halt generation like a stop sequence.

questions.q: An API can return `logprobs` for generated tokens. What are they?
options: The token IDs of alternative completions
The attention weights for each token
The number of times each token appeared in training
The log of the probability the model assigned to each generated token
questions.why: Logprobs expose model confidence per token (values ≤ 0; closer to 0 means more confident) and can include top alternatives. They are not attention weights or training-frequency counts.

questions.q: What does streaming tokens to the client primarily improve?
options: The total time to generate the full answer
Perceived latency, since users see text as soon as the first token is ready
The accuracy of the response
The GPU memory required
questions.why: Streaming does not make generation faster overall; it just shows output as it is produced, so the user waits only for TTFT before reading. Accuracy and memory are unaffected.

questions.q: Why do chat models require a specific chat template?
options: They were fine-tuned on conversations formatted with particular role markers and special tokens
Templates compress the prompt to save tokens
Templates are required by the GPU driver
Templates translate the prompt into English
questions.why: Each instruction-tuned model learned a specific layout (for example system/user/assistant headers); matching it at inference is needed for good behavior. Templates usually add tokens rather than compress the prompt.

questions.q: A developer loads Model X but encodes prompts with Model Y's tokenizer. Outputs are gibberish. Why?
options: The context window was exceeded
The temperature was too high
Token IDs map to different embeddings, so the model sees meaningless input
The KV cache was not enabled
questions.why: A model's embedding table is indexed by its own tokenizer's IDs; ID 1234 in another vocabulary is an unrelated piece of text. Always load the tokenizer from the same checkpoint as the model.

questions.q:
What does the following do?

```python
text = tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
```
options: Encodes text into IDs while dropping special tokens
Removes all punctuation from the decoded text
Truncates the IDs to the model's maximum length
Converts IDs back to text, omitting markers like BOS, EOS and padding
questions.why: `decode` maps IDs to text, and `skip_special_tokens=True` hides control tokens such as `<s>`, `</s>` or `<pad>`. Encoding is done with `encode` or by calling the tokenizer.

questions.q:
What does this return?

```python
enc = tokenizer("Hello world", return_tensors="pt")
```
options: A string of normalized text
A dict-like object containing PyTorch tensors such as `input_ids` and `attention_mask`
A list of embedding vectors
The model's logits for the input
questions.why: Hugging Face tokenizers return a `BatchEncoding`; `return_tensors="pt"` makes the values PyTorch tensors ready to pass to `model(**enc)`. Embeddings and logits come from the model, not the tokenizer.

questions.q: How is usage of hosted LLM APIs typically metered?
options: By the number of input and output tokens
By the number of words in the response only
By the number of API calls regardless of length
By the number of characters in the prompt only
questions.why: Providers usually charge per token, often with different rates for input and output tokens. Counting only the response ignores that long prompts also consume compute.

questions.q: With a GPT-style BPE tokenizer, why might "Hello" and " Hello" get different token IDs?
options: The tokenizer is case-insensitive
Spaces are always stripped before tokenization
The leading space is part of the token, so they are different vocabulary entries
One of them is treated as a special token
questions.why: Byte-level BPE folds the preceding space into word tokens (shown as `Ġ` in GPT-2), so the word at the start of text and mid-sentence are encoded differently. Spaces are preserved, not stripped.

questions.q: Why can tokenization make arithmetic harder for some LLMs?
options: Numbers are removed during preprocessing
All numbers map to the same token
Digits are treated as special tokens
Numbers may be split into inconsistent multi-digit chunks, so digit positions are not aligned
questions.why: A BPE tokenizer might encode "12345" as "123"+"45" and "12346" differently, obscuring place value. Some tokenizers split numbers into single digits or fixed-size chunks to mitigate this.

questions.q:
Which decoding strategy does this call use?

```python
out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, num_beams=1)
```
options: Top-p sampling
Greedy decoding
Beam search with 1 sample
Contrastive search
questions.why: With sampling disabled and a single beam, Hugging Face `generate` picks the argmax token each step. Beam search requires `num_beams > 1`, and sampling requires `do_sample=True`.

questions.q: A chatbot's conversation history grows beyond the model's context window. What happens if the application does nothing?
options: The request fails or older tokens are truncated, so earlier content is lost
The model automatically summarizes earlier turns
The context window expands dynamically
The model switches to a larger variant
questions.why: The window is a hard limit; servers either reject over-length input or truncate it depending on configuration. Summarizing history must be implemented by the application.

questions.q: For a single user generating tokens one at a time, what usually limits decode speed on a GPU?
options: Tokenizer speed on the CPU
The size of the vocabulary file
Memory bandwidth for reading weights and KV cache each step
Peak floating-point throughput of the Tensor Cores
questions.why: Each decode step reads all weights but does little math per byte, so it is memory-bound. Peak FLOPs matter more for prefill and large batches, which have high arithmetic intensity.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a major consumer of GPU memory when serving an LLM for inference?
options: Model weights
KV cache
Intermediate activations
Optimizer states
questions.why: Optimizer states (e.g., Adam moments) exist only during training. Inference memory is dominated by weights and the KV cache, with smaller activation buffers.

questions.q: What is the basic idea of speculative decoding?
options: Generate multiple answers and pick the most common
A small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in a single forward pass
Skip layers of the model when confident
Predict the answer length before generating
questions.why: Verifying k proposed tokens costs about the same as generating one because decode is memory-bound, so accepted tokens come almost for free. Picking the most common of several answers is self-consistency, a prompting technique.

questions.q: A model has 32 layers, hidden size 4096, standard multi-head attention, and an FP16 KV cache. Roughly how much KV cache memory does one 4,096-token sequence need?
options: 2 GiB
512 MiB
8 GiB
1 GiB
questions.why: Per token: 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 4096 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MiB; × 4,096 tokens = 2 GiB. Forgetting the factor of 2 for keys *and* values gives the tempting 1 GiB answer.

questions.q: A model uses 32 query heads but only 8 key/value heads (grouped-query attention). Compared with standard multi-head attention, how large is its KV cache?
options: The same size
Half the size
One quarter the size
One eighth the size
questions.why: The KV cache stores keys and values only for KV heads, so 8 instead of 32 heads means a 4× reduction. One eighth would confuse the number of KV heads with the reduction factor.

questions.q: An engineer must serve a 70B-parameter model on a single 80 GB GPU and keep at least 30 GB free for KV cache. Which weight precision is the highest that satisfies this?
options: FP16
FP8
INT8
INT4
questions.why: FP16 needs 140 GB (does not fit), FP8/INT8 need about 70 GB (leaving only ~10 GB), and INT4 needs about 35 GB, leaving ~45 GB for KV cache. INT8 fits the weights but violates the KV-cache requirement.

questions.q: A server runs a decode batch of 32 sequences, and each decode step takes 25 ms. What is the aggregate decode throughput?
options: 40 tokens/s
1,280 tokens/s
800 tokens/s
32 tokens/s
questions.why: Each step yields one token per sequence: 32 tokens / 0.025 s = 1,280 tokens/s. 40 tokens/s is the per-user rate (1/0.025), not the system throughput.

questions.q: A request generates 500 output tokens. End-to-end latency is 10.5 s and TTFT is 0.5 s. What is the approximate time per output token?
options: About 20 ms
About 21 ms
About 1 ms
About 50 ms
questions.why: TPOT = (total latency − TTFT) / (tokens − 1) = 10.0 s / 499 ≈ 20 ms. Dividing the full 10.5 s by 500 gives 21 ms, which wrongly includes prefill time.

questions.q: A 7B model in FP16 (≈14 GB of weights) runs at batch size 1 on a GPU with 2 TB/s memory bandwidth. What is the approximate upper bound on single-stream decode speed?
options: About 14 tokens/s
About 1,400 tokens/s
About 140 tokens/s
About 2,000 tokens/s
questions.why: Each token requires reading all weights: 14 GB ÷ 2 TB/s ≈ 7 ms, so at most ~140 tokens/s (real systems achieve somewhat less). This is why batch-1 decode speed tracks memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs.

questions.q: A weight-only INT4 model still performs matrix math in FP16 after dequantizing. Why is batch-1 decode nevertheless faster than the FP16 model?
options: INT4 reduces the number of layers
INT4 shortens the prompt
Dequantization skips the attention computation
Four times fewer weight bytes must be read from memory per token
questions.why: Batch-1 decode is memory-bandwidth bound, so cutting bytes moved is what matters; dequantization in registers is cheap relative to memory traffic. The model structure and prompt length are unchanged.

questions.q: When does W8A8 (8-bit weights and activations) quantization give a clear advantage over weight-only INT8?
options: For batch-1 latency on small models
In compute-bound workloads such as large batches and prefill, where INT8 Tensor Core GEMMs can be used
When the KV cache must be stored in FP32
When the model has no activation outliers at all and must run on CPU
questions.why: Quantizing activations too lets the matrix multiplications themselves run in INT8, raising compute throughput. In memory-bound batch-1 decode, weight-only quantization already captures most of the benefit.

questions.q: What problem does SmoothQuant address?
options: Activation outliers make activations hard to quantize, so it migrates that difficulty into the weights with per-channel scaling
Weights are too large, so it prunes half of them
The tokenizer has too many tokens
The KV cache fragments memory
questions.why: SmoothQuant divides activations by per-channel factors and multiplies the corresponding weights by them, an equivalent transformation that makes both easier to quantize to INT8 (enabling W8A8). It is not a pruning method.

questions.q: What is the key idea of AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization)?
options: Quantize activations to 4 bits using calibration data
Use second-order Hessian information to update remaining weights
Protect the small fraction of salient weights, identified by activation magnitudes, by scaling them before quantization
Train the model from scratch in INT4
questions.why: AWQ observes that channels with large activations matter most and scales them to reduce their quantization error, producing weight-only (typically INT4) models. Hessian-based error compensation is GPTQ.

questions.q: How does GPTQ quantize a model?
options: By retraining all weights with quantization-aware training
By converting only the embedding layer to INT4
By migrating activation outliers into weights
Layer by layer, using approximate second-order information to compensate the error of each quantized weight in the remaining ones
questions.why: GPTQ is a post-training method that uses a small calibration set and Hessian approximations to adjust not-yet-quantized weights. It does not require full retraining as quantization-aware training does.

questions.q: A developer using an OpenAI-compatible completions API wants the model never to output one specific token ID. Which request parameter is designed for this?
options: temperature=0
logit_bias with a large negative value for that token ID
presence_penalty=2.0
top_p=0.1
questions.why: logit_bias adds a fixed offset to the chosen tokens' logits before sampling; a value such as −100 effectively bans the token. A presence penalty applies only to tokens that have already appeared, so it cannot block the first occurrence.

questions.q: What does PagedAttention change about KV cache management?
options: It stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous, mapped by a block table
It moves the KV cache to disk
It compresses the KV cache with INT4
It recomputes keys and values instead of caching them
questions.why: Inspired by OS virtual memory paging, it allocates blocks on demand, nearly eliminating fragmentation and enabling sharing between sequences. Compression is a separate technique (KV cache quantization).

questions.q: Before PagedAttention, why did many serving systems waste a large share of KV cache memory?
options: They stored keys but not values
They kept KV caches for completed requests indefinitely
They reserved contiguous memory for each request's maximum possible length, leaving most of it unused
They duplicated the model weights per request
questions.why: Since the output length is unknown in advance, pre-reserving for max length causes internal and external fragmentation. Block-wise on-demand allocation fixes this and lets more requests fit concurrently.

questions.q: Every request to a support bot starts with the same 2,000-token system prompt. Which optimization most directly reduces TTFT?
options: Increasing temperature
Using a larger vocabulary
Enabling beam search
Prefix (prompt) caching to reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix
questions.why: If the KV entries for the common prefix are kept and reused, prefill only processes the new user tokens. The other options do not reduce prefill work, and beam search increases decode work.

questions.q: With the standard rejection-sampling verification scheme, how does the output distribution of speculative decoding compare with sampling from the large target model alone?
options: It matches the draft model's distribution
It is identical to the target model's distribution
It is an average of both models
It is always greedy
questions.why: The accept/reject rule guarantees that accepted tokens follow the target distribution, so speculative decoding is a lossless speedup. The draft model only affects speed (via acceptance rate), not output quality.

questions.q: A team adds speculative decoding but sees almost no speedup. What is the most likely cause?
options: The draft model's proposals are rarely accepted by the target model
The target model is too accurate
The prompts are too short
The tokenizer uses BPE
questions.why: Speedup depends on the acceptance rate: if the draft disagrees often, each verification step yields ~1 token while still paying draft cost. Speedups also shrink at large batch sizes where decode is already compute-bound.

questions.q: Why is beam search rarely used for open-ended chatbot responses?
options: It cannot produce an EOS token
It requires a draft model
It tends to produce generic, repetitive text and multiplies compute
It only works with character-level tokenizers
questions.why: Maximizing likelihood favors bland, safe continuations and can loop; it also runs several beams per request. Beam search remains useful for tasks with a narrow correct output such as translation.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of top-p over top-k sampling?
options: It is always deterministic
It requires no softmax
It guarantees shorter outputs
The number of candidate tokens adapts to how peaked the distribution is
questions.why: A fixed k may include junk tokens when the model is confident or exclude good options when it is uncertain; top-p sizes the candidate set dynamically. Both methods are stochastic and both operate on probabilities.

questions.q: How does min-p sampling decide which tokens to keep?
options: Keeps tokens with probability above a fixed absolute threshold
Keeps tokens whose probability is at least min_p times the top token's probability
Keeps the minimum number of tokens needed to reach probability p
Keeps the k least probable tokens
questions.why: The threshold scales with the model's confidence: a confident step prunes aggressively, a flat step keeps many options. Option C describes top-p.

questions.q: How does a frequency penalty differ from a presence penalty?
options: Frequency penalty grows with how many times a token has appeared; presence penalty is a flat penalty once it has appeared at all
Frequency penalty applies to prompt tokens only; presence penalty to output only
Frequency penalty raises temperature; presence penalty lowers it
They are identical names for the same mechanism
questions.why: Frequency penalty discourages verbatim repetition proportional to count, while presence penalty nudges the model toward new topics. Neither changes temperature.

questions.q: The logits for three tokens are [3, 1, 0]. What is the approximate softmax probability of the first token?
questions.why: e³ ≈ 20.09, e¹ ≈ 2.72, e⁰ = 1; 20.09 / 23.81 ≈ 0.84. Dividing the raw logits by their sum (3/4 = 0.75) is the tempting mistake because it ignores the exponential.

questions.q: Two tokens have logits [2, 0]. At temperature 1.0 the first token has probability ≈ 0.88. What is its probability at temperature 2.0?
options: About 0.95
About 0.50
About 0.88
About 0.73
questions.why: Dividing by T = 2 gives logits [1, 0]; softmax yields e/(e+1) ≈ 0.73. Higher temperature flattens the distribution, so the answer must fall below 0.88, ruling out 0.95.

questions.q: Sorted next-token probabilities are [0.50, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05]. With top_p = 0.8, how many tokens remain in the sampling pool?
questions.why: Cumulative sums are 0.50, 0.70, 0.85; the nucleus is the smallest set reaching 0.8, so three tokens are kept. Stopping at two tokens (0.70) would fall short of the threshold.

questions.q: Which sampling setting makes `do_sample=True` behave like greedy decoding?
options: top_k = 1
top_p = 1.0
temperature = 1.0
repetition_penalty = 1.0
questions.why: Keeping only the single most probable token leaves nothing to sample but the argmax. top_p = 1.0 and temperature = 1.0 leave the full distribution unchanged, which is the opposite of greedy.

questions.q:
A developer runs this and finds the printed answer starts with the full prompt:

```python
inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0]))
```

What is the correct fix?
options: Set `skip_special_tokens=True`
Set `do_sample=True`
Decode only `out[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]`
Lower `max_new_tokens`
questions.why: For decoder-only models, `generate` returns the prompt tokens followed by the new tokens, so slicing off the prompt length leaves only the completion. Skipping special tokens removes markers like EOS but not the prompt text.

questions.q: A developer batches prompts of different lengths for a decoder-only model and gets poor completions for the shorter prompts. Which tokenizer setting is most likely needed?
options: `truncation=True`
`padding_side="right"`
`add_special_tokens=False`
`padding_side="left"`
questions.why: Decoder-only models append new tokens at the end of each row, so padding must go on the left; with right padding the model would continue generating after pad tokens. Right padding is fine for encoder models and training, but not for batched generation.

questions.q: Calling `tokenizer(batch, padding=True)` on a Llama-family tokenizer raises an error that no padding token is defined. What is the common fix?
options: Set `padding=False` and truncate all inputs to 1 token
Set `tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token`
Switch to a WordPiece tokenizer
Increase `model_max_length`
questions.why: Many decoder-only tokenizers ship without a pad token; reusing EOS is standard because the attention mask hides pad positions anyway. Changing tokenizer type would break compatibility with the model.

questions.q: A developer pads a batch but passes only `input_ids` (no `attention_mask`) to the model. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The model attends to pad tokens, so outputs for padded sequences are degraded
The model raises an out-of-memory error
Generation becomes deterministic
The KV cache is disabled
questions.why: Without the mask, pad positions are treated as real tokens and contaminate attention (Hugging Face often warns about this). Memory use and determinism are not affected by the missing mask.

questions.q:
What does `add_generation_prompt=True` do here?

```python
text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
```
options: Adds a default system prompt
Appends an EOS token to end the conversation
Generates a response from the model
Appends the header that starts an assistant turn so the model replies as the assistant
questions.why: The template formats messages with role markers; this flag adds the assistant-turn prefix (e.g., `<|im_start|>assistant`) so generation begins in the right place. It only formats text; it does not call the model.

questions.q: An instruction-tuned model, prompted with plain text instead of its chat template, keeps writing new "User:" questions after answering. What is the most likely cause?
options: Temperature is set to 0
The context window is too large
The prompt format does not match the template the model was tuned on
The KV cache is too small
questions.why: Without the expected role tokens, the model does not know where its turn ends and may never emit its end-of-turn token, continuing the transcript instead. Using `apply_chat_template` usually fixes this.

questions.q: An engineer must verify that a prompt fits a model's context window before sending it. What is the most reliable method?
options: Divide the character count by 4
Count tokens with the target model's own tokenizer
Count words and multiply by 1.3
Use any open-source tokenizer such as GPT-2's
questions.why: Heuristics are fine for estimates, but token counts vary by tokenizer and language, so exact checks need the model's tokenizer (plus chat-template overhead). Another model's tokenizer can be off by a large margin.

questions.q: A model has an 8,192-token context window. The prompt (with chat template) is 7,000 tokens. What is the largest `max_new_tokens` that avoids exceeding the window?
questions.why: Input and output share the window: 8,192 − 7,000 = 1,192 tokens remain. Requesting 2,048 new tokens would overflow and either error or be truncated.

questions.q: A tokenizer needs about 3× more tokens per word for Hindi than for English. If a prompt budget fits roughly 3,000 English words, about how many Hindi words fit?
questions.why: The token budget is fixed, so tripling tokens per word cuts the word capacity to one third. 9,000 inverts the relationship.

questions.q: A model has a 128,000-token vocabulary and hidden size 4,096. How many parameters does the input embedding matrix alone contain?
options: About 32 million
About 128 million
About 4 billion
About 524 million
questions.why: The embedding table is vocab × hidden = 128,000 × 4,096 ≈ 524M parameters; an untied output projection adds the same again. This is why very large vocabularies noticeably increase model size.

questions.q: A SentencePiece tokenizer with byte fallback encounters an emoji not in its vocabulary. What happens?
options: It is replaced by `<unk>`
It is encoded as a sequence of UTF-8 byte tokens
It is silently removed
It is mapped to the nearest emoji in the vocabulary
questions.why: Byte fallback (used by Llama 2 and others) guarantees lossless encoding by falling back to byte-level tokens such as `<0xF0>`. Without byte fallback, the character would become `<unk>`.

questions.q: In the Hugging Face `tokenizers` library, in what order do the pipeline stages run when encoding text?
options: Normalization → pre-tokenization → model (e.g., BPE) → post-processing
Pre-tokenization → normalization → post-processing → model
Model → normalization → pre-tokenization → post-processing
Post-processing → model → pre-tokenization → normalization
questions.why: Text is first cleaned (Unicode normalization, lowercasing), then split into words, then the subword model segments them, and finally post-processing adds special tokens such as `[CLS]`/`[SEP]`. Adding special tokens must come last so they are not split.

questions.q: A developer needs to highlight in the original text which characters correspond to each token for an NER display. Which tokenizer option helps?
options: `return_attention_mask=True`
`return_token_type_ids=True`
`return_offsets_mapping=True`
`return_overflowing_tokens=True`
questions.why: Fast (Rust-backed) tokenizers return (start, end) character spans per token, allowing exact alignment back to the source text. Token type IDs only mark sentence A/B segments.

questions.q: A completion prompt ends with "The capital of France is " (with a trailing space), and output quality drops. Why?
options: Trailing spaces exceed the context window
Words are usually tokenized with their leading space, so ending on a bare space forces an unusual token boundary
Spaces are converted to EOS tokens
The tokenizer lowercases text after a space
questions.why: The natural continuation is the token " Paris" (space included); a standalone space token followed by "Paris" is rare in training data. Removing the trailing space (or "token healing") avoids the problem.

questions.q: How does grammar- or schema-constrained decoding enforce valid output?
options: It retries generation until the output parses
It fine-tunes the model on JSON examples
It post-processes the text with a repair function
At each step it masks the logits of tokens that would violate the grammar
questions.why: A state machine tracks where the output is in the grammar and sets invalid tokens' logits to −∞, so only valid continuations can be sampled. Retrying or repairing works after the fact and offers no guarantee.

questions.q: An extraction service returns malformed JSON in 3% of responses despite careful prompting. Which approach guarantees syntactically valid JSON?
options: Structured output via JSON-schema-constrained decoding
Raising the temperature
Adding more few-shot examples
Using beam search with 8 beams
questions.why: Constraining the token choices to the schema makes invalid syntax impossible. More examples or beams improve the odds but cannot guarantee validity, and higher temperature makes errors more likely.

questions.q: A three-token answer has token logprobs of −0.1, −0.2 and −0.7. What is the probability the model assigned to the whole answer?
options: About 0.33
About 0.70
About 0.10
About 0.37
questions.why: Log-probabilities add across tokens: −0.1 − 0.2 − 0.7 = −1.0, and e^−1 ≈ 0.37. Averaging the logprobs (−0.33) would give a per-token figure, not the sequence probability.

questions.q: A completion endpoint answers correctly but then continues with "\nUser: ..." and invents the next turn. What is the simplest fix at inference time?
options: Increase the repetition penalty
Add "\nUser:" as a stop sequence
Use top_k = 1
Increase the context window
questions.why: A stop sequence halts generation exactly where the next turn would begin. Greedy decoding would still produce the invented turn if it is the most likely continuation, and repetition penalties do not target turn boundaries.

questions.q: What does `no_repeat_ngram_size=3` do in Hugging Face `generate`?
options: Prevents any 3-token sequence from appearing more than once in the output
Penalizes each token after it repeats 3 times
Stops generation after 3 repeated sentences
Limits each sentence to 3 words
questions.why: It hard-blocks tokens that would complete an already-seen trigram, eliminating loops but sometimes blocking legitimate repeats like names. A soft score reduction is a repetition penalty instead.

questions.q: Why is the prefill phase usually compute-bound while decode is memory-bound?
options: Prefill does not use the KV cache
Prefill runs on the CPU
Prefill processes many tokens per weight read, giving high arithmetic intensity
Prefill uses lower precision
questions.why: Hundreds or thousands of prompt tokens are multiplied by each weight matrix at once (matrix-matrix work), so FLOPs dominate. Decode handles one token per sequence per step, so loading weights dominates; prefill does write the KV cache.

questions.q: A forward pass costs roughly 2 × (number of parameters) FLOPs per token. Approximately how many FLOPs does prefill of a 1,000-token prompt on a 7B model require (ignoring attention)?
options: 7 TFLOPs
14 GFLOPs
14 TFLOPs
140 TFLOPs
questions.why: 2 × 7×10⁹ × 1,000 = 1.4×10¹³ FLOPs = 14 TFLOPs. 14 GFLOPs is the cost of a single token, and 7 TFLOPs forgets the factor of 2 (multiply and add).

questions.q: While one user submits a 30,000-token prompt, other users' streams stall. Which scheduling technique addresses this?
options: Beam search
Chunked prefill, splitting the long prompt into pieces interleaved with decode steps
Increasing max_new_tokens
Static batching
questions.why: Processing a huge prompt in one step blocks decode iterations for everyone; chunking bounds each step's work so ongoing streams keep receiving tokens. Static batching would make the stall worse.

questions.q: What typically happens when an inference server's maximum batch size is increased?
options: Throughput rises but per-request latency also rises
Both throughput and latency improve without limit
Throughput falls but latency improves
Neither changes because decode is compute-bound
questions.why: Larger batches amortize weight reads, increasing total tokens/s, but each step takes longer and more requests share the GPU, so each user sees slower tokens. Gains flatten once the GPU becomes compute-bound or KV memory runs out.

questions.q: An 80 GB GPU holds a model with 14 GB of FP16 weights. Each token's KV cache uses 0.5 MiB, and every request uses 2,048 tokens. Ignoring activations and overhead, about how many requests can run concurrently?
questions.why: Each request needs 2,048 × 0.5 MiB = 1 GiB of KV cache; 80 − 14 = 66 GB remain, so roughly 66 requests (fewer in practice after runtime overhead). 80 ignores the memory used by the weights.

questions.q: If the context length served per request doubles, what happens to KV cache memory and prefill attention compute?
options: Both double
Both quadruple
KV memory quadruples; attention compute doubles
KV memory doubles; attention compute roughly quadruples
questions.why: The cache stores one K/V entry per token (linear), while full self-attention over n tokens computes n² scores (quadratic). This is why long-context serving stresses both memory and compute.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of storing the KV cache in FP8 instead of FP16?
options: It removes the need for prefill
It halves KV memory, allowing longer contexts or more concurrent requests
It makes the model weights smaller
It improves the model's accuracy
questions.why: KV cache quantization is independent of weight quantization and directly increases how many tokens fit in memory. It usually costs a small amount of accuracy rather than improving it.

questions.q: A model trained with RoPE on 4K contexts must handle 16K tokens. What does linear position interpolation do?
options: Scales position indices down by 4× so 16K positions map into the trained 0–4K range
Adds learned absolute position embeddings for positions beyond 4K
Truncates the input to the last 4K tokens
Increases the number of attention heads
questions.why: Compressing positions keeps rotation angles within the familiar range, typically followed by brief fine-tuning. Truncation would discard content instead of extending context.

questions.q: A RoPE model trained on 4K tokens is run on an 8K prompt with no scaling. What is the most likely result?
options: Output quality is unchanged
The model automatically compresses the prompt
Quality degrades sharply once positions exceed the trained range
The KV cache is automatically halved
questions.why: Unseen rotation angles push attention out of distribution, often producing incoherent text or perplexity blow-ups beyond the trained length. Context extension methods like RoPE scaling exist precisely to avoid this.

questions.q: A long-running chat exceeds the context window. Which strategy best preserves behavior while staying within limits?
options: Drop the system prompt first
Keep the system prompt and most recent turns, dropping or summarizing the oldest turns
Randomly remove 25% of tokens
Keep only the first user message
questions.why: The system prompt carries persistent instructions and recent turns carry immediate context, so oldest turns are the cheapest to sacrifice. Dropping the system prompt silently changes the assistant's behavior.

questions.q: A batch job has 100 requests, each producing 200 output tokens. The server sustains 2,000 output tokens/s aggregate. Ignoring prefill, roughly how long does the job take?
options: 1 s
questions.why: Total output is 100 × 200 = 20,000 tokens; 20,000 / 2,000 tokens/s = 10 s. 100 s would follow from processing requests one at a time at 200 tokens/s each.

questions.q: A marketing team wants varied slogan ideas without incoherent, rare-word outputs. Which settings fit best?
options: temperature 0.9 with top_p 0.9
temperature 0 with beam search
temperature 2.0 with no truncation
greedy decoding with a repetition penalty
questions.why: Moderately high temperature adds diversity while the nucleus cutoff removes the long tail of unlikely tokens. Temperature 2.0 without truncation samples too many junk tokens, while greedy or beam search gives the same output every time.

questions.q:
What does this call return?

```python
out = model.generate(**inputs, num_beams=4, num_return_sequences=2,
                     do_sample=False)
```
options: Four sequences, one per beam
Two sampled sequences
The two highest-scoring of the four final beams
One sequence repeated twice
questions.why: Beam search keeps 4 hypotheses and `num_return_sequences` (which must be ≤ `num_beams`) selects the top 2 by score. No sampling happens because `do_sample=False`.

questions.q: In Hugging Face beam search, what does setting `length_penalty` above 1.0 do?
options: Forces outputs to stop earlier
Favors longer sequences
Penalizes repeated tokens
Limits the beam width
questions.why: Beam scores are sum of log-probs divided by length^length_penalty; since log-probs are negative, a larger exponent shrinks the penalty for long sequences more. Values below 1.0 favor shorter outputs.

questions.q: A model frequently emits EOS immediately and returns empty answers. Which generation parameter prevents this directly?
options: max_new_tokens
top_k
repetition_penalty
min_new_tokens
questions.why: `min_new_tokens` suppresses the EOS token until a minimum number of tokens has been produced. `max_new_tokens` sets an upper bound and does nothing about early stopping.

questions.q: After supervised fine-tuning, a model keeps generating until it hits max_new_tokens on every request, often inventing extra conversation turns. What is the most likely cause?
options: The temperature is set too low
The KV cache is too small
The training targets did not end with an EOS token, so the model never learned to stop
The tokenizer vocabulary is too large
questions.why: Models learn when to stop by predicting EOS at the end of training targets; if formatting omitted EOS or masked it out of the loss, the model rarely emits it. Low temperature makes outputs more deterministic but would not suppress an EOS the model actually predicts.

questions.q: A 70B model has 80 layers, 8 KV heads with head dimension 128 (grouped-query attention), and an FP16 KV cache. How much KV cache does one 8,192-token sequence need?
options: 1.25 GiB
20 GiB
2.5 GiB
5 GiB
questions.why: Per token: 2 (K,V) × 80 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB; × 8,192 tokens = 2.5 GiB. With 64 KV heads (full MHA) it would be 8× larger (20 GiB), and omitting the K/V factor of 2 gives 1.25 GiB.

questions.q: In speculative decoding the draft proposes γ = 4 tokens, and each is accepted independently with probability α = 0.8. Using E = (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α), how many tokens are produced per target-model verification pass on average?
options: About 3.36
questions.why: (1 − 0.8⁵) / 0.2 = (1 − 0.328) / 0.2 ≈ 3.36, which counts accepted draft tokens plus the one token the target always contributes (a correction or bonus token). 3.2 (α × γ) ignores both the bonus token and the fact that acceptance stops at the first rejection.

questions.q: In speculative sampling with draft distribution q and target distribution p, how is a drafted token x handled?
options: Accepted only if it is the target's argmax
Accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on rejection, a token is resampled from the normalized max(0, p − q)
Always accepted if q(x) > 0.5
Accepted with probability q(x)/p(x); on rejection, the draft model resamples
questions.why: This modified rejection sampling makes the final token distribution exactly p, which is why the method is lossless. Requiring argmax agreement is a greedy-only variant and would not preserve sampling behavior.

questions.q: Medusa-style decoding accelerates generation without a separate draft model. How?
options: Extra lightweight decoding heads on the base model predict several future tokens, verified together with tree attention
It skips every second transformer layer
It caches whole responses from previous users
It quantizes the model to 2 bits during decode
questions.why: The heads read the last hidden state and guess tokens at positions t+2, t+3, …; candidates are verified in one forward pass. Layer skipping is a different (early-exit) approach.

questions.q: For which workload is n-gram "prompt lookup" speculative decoding especially effective?
options: Open-ended creative story writing
Translation into a language absent from the prompt
Code editing or document summarization where outputs copy long spans from the input
Generating random numbers
questions.why: The draft is produced by matching the latest n-gram against the prompt and proposing the tokens that followed it, so it shines when outputs reuse input text. In creative writing, matches are rare and acceptance is low.

questions.q: With PagedAttention block size 16, how many token slots are wasted for a single sequence of 1,000 tokens?
questions.why: 1,000 / 16 = 62.5, so 63 blocks (1,008 slots) are allocated and only the last block is partially filled: 8 slots unused. Waste is bounded by one block per sequence, unlike max-length pre-allocation.

questions.q: A request asks for 4 parallel samples from the same prompt. How does a PagedAttention-based server avoid storing the prompt's KV cache four times?
options: It recomputes the prompt for each sample
Samples share the prompt's physical blocks via reference counts, copying a block only when a sample writes to it
It stores the prompt KV cache on the CPU
It generates the samples sequentially
questions.why: Block tables of different sequences can point to the same physical blocks; copy-on-write happens only for the partially filled block where they diverge. The same mechanism helps beam search.

questions.q: For batch-1 decode with FP16 weights, each weight (2 bytes) is used in one multiply-add (2 FLOPs). What is the approximate arithmetic intensity of the weight GEMVs?
options: About 1 FLOP per byte
About 0.25 FLOP per byte
About 100 FLOPs per byte
About 300 FLOPs per byte
questions.why: 2 FLOPs / 2 bytes ≈ 1 FLOP/byte, while a modern data-center GPU needs on the order of hundreds of FLOPs per byte to be compute-bound. That gap is why batch-1 decode leaves most Tensor Core capacity idle.

questions.q: Larger decode batches amortize weight reads, yet attention time still grows roughly linearly with batch size at long contexts. Why?
options: Attention weights are recomputed for each token in the vocabulary
Attention runs on the CPU
Each sequence has its own KV cache, so KV reads are not shared across the batch
Softmax cannot be batched
questions.why: Weights are common to all sequences, but each sequence attends over its private keys and values, so memory traffic scales with batch × context. Long-context, high-batch decode is therefore often KV-bandwidth bound.

questions.q: A team finds that a weight-only INT4 model is faster than FP16 at batch 1 but slower than an FP8 model at batch 256. What best explains this?
options: INT4 models cannot use a KV cache
INT4 models have more layers
At large batch the GPU is memory-bound, which INT4 cannot help
At large batch the workload is compute-bound, and dequantizing INT4 to FP16 adds overhead without faster math, unlike native FP8 GEMMs
questions.why: Weight-only quantization saves bandwidth, which matters when memory-bound; once compute dominates, FP8 (W8A8) Tensor Core math wins. Option C reverses which regime large batches are in.

questions.q: A model is quantized to INT4 with one FP16 scale per group of 128 weights (no zero-point). What is the effective storage per weight?
options: 4.0 bits
4.125 bits
4.5 bits
5.0 bits
questions.why: Each group adds 16 bits of scale spread over 128 weights: 4 + 16/128 = 4.125 bits. Smaller groups (e.g., 32) improve accuracy but raise overhead to 4.5 bits.

questions.q: Why does naive per-tensor INT8 quantization of LLM activations often hurt accuracy badly in large models?
options: A few channels have very large outlier values, so a single scale wastes most of the range on them and crushes the other values
Activations are always negative
INT8 cannot represent zero
Activations change only during training
questions.why: Systematic outlier features emerge in large transformers; per-tensor scaling then leaves typical values with only a few quantization levels. Remedies include SmoothQuant, mixed-precision decomposition (LLM.int8()), and finer-grained scales.

questions.q: How do the FP8 formats E4M3 and E5M2 differ in typical use?
options: E4M3 is integer-based; E5M2 is floating point
E5M2 has more precision and is used for weights
E4M3 has more mantissa precision and suits weights/activations in inference; E5M2 has more range and suits gradients
They are identical except for byte order
questions.why: Four exponent bits and three mantissa bits trade range for precision, which suits forward-pass tensors; five exponent bits give the dynamic range gradients need. Both are floating-point formats.

questions.q: What is required to use static (pre-computed) activation scales in INT8 or FP8 inference?
options: Retraining the model from scratch
A larger tokenizer vocabulary
Disabling the KV cache
A representative calibration dataset to measure activation ranges
questions.why: Static quantization fixes scales ahead of time from statistics collected on sample inputs; unrepresentative calibration data leads to clipping or poor resolution. Dynamic quantization computes scales at runtime instead, at some overhead.

questions.q: How does NTK-aware RoPE scaling differ from linear position interpolation?
options: It removes positional information entirely
It increases the RoPE base frequency, stretching low-frequency dimensions while largely preserving high-frequency ones
It divides all positions by the same factor
It adds a learned embedding per new position
questions.why: Linear interpolation compresses every frequency equally, blurring nearby-token distinctions; changing the base keeps local resolution and often works reasonably even without fine-tuning. Option C describes linear interpolation itself.

questions.q: What does YaRN add on top of frequency-based RoPE interpolation?
options: Per-dimension ("by parts") interpolation plus an attention temperature adjustment, allowing extension with little fine-tuning
A second tokenizer for long documents
Sliding-window attention with a fixed window
Absolute learned position embeddings
questions.why: YaRN interpolates low-frequency dimensions, leaves high-frequency ones mostly intact, and rescales attention logits to counter entropy changes at long range. It remains a RoPE method, not a switch to learned absolute embeddings.

questions.q: StreamingLLM lets a model generate over very long streams with a bounded KV cache. What does it keep in the cache?
options: Only the most recent tokens in a sliding window
Every 10th token
The KV entries of the first few tokens (attention sinks) plus a sliding window of recent tokens
A compressed summary vector of all tokens
questions.why: Models dump a lot of attention mass onto initial tokens; evicting them destabilizes generation, so keeping a few "sink" tokens plus a recent window keeps output fluent. A pure sliding window, option A, is what breaks.

questions.q: Why do some large deployments run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools (disaggregated serving)?
options: Decode requires FP32 while prefill uses INT4
Tokenization must run on dedicated GPUs
Prefill does not need the model weights
The phases have different bottlenecks, and separating them avoids interference and allows tuning each pool, at the cost of transferring the KV cache
questions.why: Compute-heavy prefill bursts inflate decode latency when co-located; separate pools can use different parallelism and batch sizes for TTFT and TPOT targets. Both phases need the full model weights.

questions.q: A paged-KV server runs out of free blocks mid-generation as sequences grow. What do schedulers like vLLM typically do?
options: Crash the server
Preempt some sequences, freeing their blocks by swapping them to CPU memory or discarding them for later recomputation
Truncate every sequence to half its length
Switch all sequences to greedy decoding
questions.why: Preempted requests are resumed later, either by swapping their KV blocks back or by re-running prefill over prompt plus generated tokens. Truncation would corrupt outputs.

questions.q: A static batch holds 4 requests whose outputs are 100, 100, 100 and 1,000 tokens. The batch runs until the longest finishes. What fraction of decode slot-steps does useful work?
questions.why: Useful work is 100+100+100+1,000 = 1,300 token-steps out of 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 slot-steps, or 32.5%. Continuous batching recovers the idle slots by admitting new requests as the short ones finish.

questions.q: Without prefix sharing, how does beam search with width 4 affect KV cache memory compared with greedy decoding for one request?
options: No change, since beams share one cache
It doubles
It grows about 4×
It grows 16×
questions.why: Each beam is a separate sequence with its own keys and values, so memory scales with beam width. Paged block sharing can reduce the duplicated prompt portion, but a naive implementation stores all four.

questions.q:
What is the effect of this custom logits processor during generation?

```python
class Ban(LogitsProcessor):
    def __init__(self, ids): self.ids = ids
    def __call__(self, input_ids, scores):
        scores[:, self.ids] = -float("inf")
        return scores
```
options: It lowers the temperature for the listed tokens
It forces the listed tokens to be generated next
It removes the listed tokens from the prompt
The listed tokens get zero probability and can never be generated
questions.why: Setting logits to −∞ makes their softmax probability exactly zero for both greedy and sampled decoding. This is the same masking primitive used by `bad_words_ids` and constrained decoding.

questions.q: In a pipeline that applies temperature before top-p filtering, what happens to the nucleus when temperature is raised from 0.7 to 1.3 (top_p fixed at 0.9)?
options: It stays the same because top-p ignores temperature
It contains more tokens because the flatter distribution needs more tokens to reach 0.9
It contains fewer tokens
It always contains exactly one token
questions.why: Higher temperature spreads probability mass, so the cumulative threshold is reached later and more candidates survive. This compounding is why combining high temperature with permissive top-p can quickly produce incoherent text.

questions.q: Next-token probabilities are [0.60, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05, 0.05] and min_p = 0.25. How many tokens remain eligible?
questions.why: The threshold is relative: 0.25 × 0.60 = 0.15, so only 0.60 and 0.20 survive. Treating 0.25 as an absolute cutoff would keep just one token, which is the tempting mistake.

questions.q: The CTRL-style repetition penalty divides a repeated token's logit by the penalty when it is positive but multiplies it when negative. Why?
options: Negative logits are invalid and must be removed
Multiplying is faster than dividing on GPUs
Dividing a negative logit by a penalty > 1 would increase it, making the token more likely instead of less
It keeps the softmax sum equal to 1
questions.why: For example −2 / 1.2 ≈ −1.67, which is higher; multiplying gives −2.4, which correctly lowers it. Softmax normalization is unaffected by this choice.

questions.q: Using logit' = logit − count × frequency_penalty − (count > 0) × presence_penalty, a token has appeared 3 times with frequency_penalty 0.5 and presence_penalty 0.6. By how much is its logit reduced?
questions.why: The frequency term is 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 and the presence term adds a flat 0.6, for 2.1 in total. Multiplying the presence penalty by the count (3.3) is the common mistake.

questions.q: Why can't a JSON grammar be enforced by checking characters one at a time during decoding?
options: JSON grammars cannot be expressed as state machines
Tokens span multiple characters and may cross grammar boundaries, so valid next tokens must be computed by mapping the grammar state onto the vocabulary
Logits cannot be masked on GPUs
Tokenizers remove braces and quotes
questions.why: A token like `"},` advances the grammar several steps at once; libraries precompute, per grammar state, which vocabulary tokens are allowed. Regular and context-free JSON grammars are readily expressed as automata.

questions.q: What is a known risk of strict constrained decoding?
options: Forcing tokens the model considers unlikely can distort the distribution and lower content quality
It always produces invalid syntax
It disables the KV cache
It increases the vocabulary size
questions.why: When the schema conflicts with what the model would naturally write (e.g., field order, no room to reason), the model may be pushed into low-probability, lower-quality content. Syntax is guaranteed valid, so B is the opposite of the actual behavior.

questions.q: A streaming client decodes each byte-level BPE token independently and occasionally shows "�" characters for emoji and Chinese text. What is the fix?
options: Switch to greedy decoding
Increase max_new_tokens
Buffer tokens and emit text only once complete UTF-8 characters can be decoded
Lowercase the output
questions.why: A multi-byte character may be split across tokens, so decoding a single token yields an invalid partial sequence. Incremental detokenizers hold back incomplete bytes until the next token completes them.

questions.q: Some tokenizers deliberately split numbers into individual digits (or fixed short chunks). What is the main motivation?
options: To shrink the vocabulary to fewer than 100 tokens
To prevent numbers from being generated
To reduce sequence length for numeric text
To give numbers a consistent representation aligned with place value, improving arithmetic
questions.why: Ad-hoc BPE merges make similar numbers tokenize very differently; consistent digit splitting helps the model learn arithmetic patterns. It actually increases sequence length for numbers, the opposite of option C.

questions.q: How does a WordPiece tokenizer segment a word at inference time?
options: By applying learned merges in priority order
By greedily taking the longest vocabulary prefix, then repeating on the remainder with `##` pieces
By sampling among possible segmentations
By Viterbi search for the most probable segmentation under a unigram model
questions.why: BERT's WordPiece uses greedy longest-match-first; if no piece matches, the whole word becomes `[UNK]`. Applying ranked merges is BPE, and Viterbi decoding is Unigram.

questions.q: What is subword regularization with a Unigram tokenizer?
options: Sampling different segmentations of the same text during training to make the model robust to tokenization variation
Penalizing long tokens in the loss
Removing rare tokens from the vocabulary after training
Applying dropout to the embedding layer
questions.why: Because Unigram defines a probability over segmentations, it can sample alternatives (BPE-dropout plays a similar role for BPE). At inference the most likely segmentation is typically used.

questions.q: Certain rare vocabulary entries (e.g., odd usernames) make a model output bizarre text when they appear in a prompt. What is the likely cause?
options: The tokens exceed the context window
The tokens are special control tokens
They were in the tokenizer's training data but almost absent from the model's training data, so their embeddings are under-trained
They are encoded as bytes
questions.why: When tokenizer and model corpora differ, some tokens exist but are rarely seen in training, leaving near-random embeddings ("glitch tokens"). Byte tokens are common and well-trained.

questions.q: A team sees slightly different outputs for the same prompt with temperature 0 on a busy inference server. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: Temperature 0 still samples randomly
The tokenizer is nondeterministic
The KV cache is shared between users
Batch composition changes kernel execution and floating-point reduction order, and near-ties in logits can flip the argmax
questions.why: Floating-point addition is not associative, so different batch sizes or kernels yield tiny numeric differences that can change a greedy choice and then the rest of the output. Tokenization of the same string is deterministic.

questions.q: A 13B model has 40 layers and hidden size 5,120 (standard MHA, FP16 KV cache). What is the KV cache for a batch of 16 sequences of 4,096 tokens each?
options: About 25 GiB
About 50 GiB
About 100 GiB
About 3 GiB
questions.why: Per token: 2 × 40 × 5,120 × 2 bytes = 800 KiB; × 65,536 tokens = 50 GiB. Added to 26 GB of FP16 weights, this would not fit comfortably on an 80 GB GPU; about 3 GiB is the figure for one sequence only.

questions.q: A server prefills at 10,000 tokens/s and decodes a single stream at 50 tokens/s. Ignoring queueing, how long does a request with an 8,000-token prompt and 200 output tokens take?
options: About 4.8 s
About 4.0 s
About 0.8 s
About 160 s
questions.why: Prefill takes 8,000 / 10,000 = 0.8 s (the TTFT), and decoding 200 tokens at 50 tokens/s takes 4 s, for about 4.8 s. 4.0 s forgets prefill entirely, and 160 s wrongly decodes the prompt at decode speed.

questions.q: A Mixture-of-Experts model has about 47B total parameters but activates about 13B per token. Which statement about inference is correct?
options: It needs memory for only the 13B active parameters
It has the compute cost of a 47B dense model per token
It must hold all ~47B parameters in memory, but per-token compute is closer to a ~13B dense model
It cannot use a KV cache
questions.why: Any expert might be routed to, so all experts must be resident, while each token only runs through the selected experts. At large batch, different tokens hit different experts, so memory traffic can approach that of the full model.

questions.q: After `tokenizer.add_special_tokens({"additional_special_tokens": ["<tool>"]})`, running the model on inputs containing `<tool>` throws an index error. What was missed?
options: Setting `padding_side="left"`
Re-saving the tokenizer to disk
Setting `skip_special_tokens=True`
Calling `model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))`
questions.why: The new token gets an ID beyond the embedding table's size, so the lookup is out of range until the embedding (and output) matrices are resized. The new rows start untrained, so the token usually needs fine-tuning to be useful.
